content: 1. In the past three months, have you received counseling on the use of condoms and safe sexual practices? This could include services provided by outreach programs, drop-in centers, or sexual health clinics. 2. Have you undergone testing for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) within the last three months? This question specifically applies to sex workers, transgender individuals, and men who have sex with men. 3. For individuals who inject drugs: Have you received new, sterile needles and syringes in the past three months? 4. The numerator refers to the number of individuals in a key population who have received a defined, evidence-based package of HIV prevention interventions. 5. The denominator is the estimated size of the key population group. 6. Measurement methods for the numerator include program data, such as registers and service logs. The HIV prevention interventions measured should align with the nationally defined, evidence-based package for each key population. 7. For people who inject drugs, the prevention package must include access to sterile needles and syringes. 8. The denominator is validated through population size estimates relevant to the program of interest. 9. Disaggregation of data should include gender (male, female, transgender), age (<25 years, 25+ years), and type of provider (public sector, key population-led organizations, private for-profit or not-for-profit entities, including faith-based and international NGOs). 10. The number of needles and syringes distributed per year per person who injects drugs measures whether programs provide sufficient sterile injecting equipment to meet the needs of this population. 11. When measured against the estimated number of people who inject drugs, this indicator helps assess national progress toward coverage of needle-syringe programs (NSPs). 12. When measured against the number of people reached by NSPs in the last 12 months, it evaluates the quality of NSPs and whether adequate sterile needles and syringes are being distributed. 13. The numerator is the number of sterile needles and syringes distributed by NSPs during the reporting period. 14. The population-based denominator is the number of people in the country who inject drugs. 15. The program-based denominator is the number of people who inject drugs reached by NSPs during the reporting period. 16. Measurement methods for the numerator include program registers and NSP logbooks. For the population-based denominator, size estimation exercises are used. For the program-based denominator, program registers and NSP logbooks are utilized. 17. The recommended reporting period is 12 months. 18. Disaggregation includes gender (male, female, transgender), age (<25 years, 25+ years), type of setting (community, prison/closed setting), and provider type (public sector, key population-led organization, other). 19. The percentage of people who inject drugs receiving opioid substitution therapy (OST) measures the program’s ability to deliver OST to opioid-dependent individuals who inject drugs. 20. OST is a critical component of harm reduction services, as it directly reduces the number of injection risk acts per person who injects drugs. 21. The numerator is the number of people who inject drugs and are on OST at a specified date during the reporting period. 22. The denominator is the number of opioid-dependent people in the country who inject drugs. 23. Measurement methods for the numerator include program registers and OST registers. For the denominator, size estimation exercises are used. 24. Caution must be taken to include only opioid-dependent individuals who inject drugs in both the numerator and denominator, as not all OST recipients have a history of injecting, and not all people who inject drugs are opioid-dependent. 25. Disaggregation includes gender (male, female, transgender) and age (<25 years, 25+ years). 26. The percentage of people who inject drugs who report using sterile injecting equipment the last time they injected measures progress in preventing HIV transmission associated with injecting drug use. 27. The risk of HIV transmission through contaminated injecting equipment is extremely high. 28. Safer injecting practices, such as using new or sterile injecting equipment, are critical to reducing transmission risk. 29. Measures of injecting practices at the last injection provide a proxy for the proportion of injection acts in which sterile injecting equipment is used. 30. The numerator is the number of survey respondents who answer “yes” to both of the following questions: Have you injected drugs at any time in the past month? The last time you injected drugs, did you use a sterile needle and syringe? 31. The denominator is the number of survey respondents. 32. Measurement methods include representative surveys of people who inject drugs, such as BBS, BSS, and HSS+. 33. Disaggregation includes gender (male, female, transgender) and age (<25 years, 25+ years). 34. The percentage of adolescent girls and young women seeking contraception or family planning services who received an HIV test measures the integration of HIV testing with sexual and reproductive health services. 35. Adolescent girls and young women seeking contraception or family planning services often engage in unprotected sexual intercourse, putting them at risk for HIV infection in high-burden settings. 36. The Evidence for Contraceptive Options in HIV Outcomes (ECHO) trial showed a high incidence of HIV infection among all women seeking contraception, especially those under 25 years. 37. In high HIV burden settings, programs should strengthen the integration of HIV prevention with contraceptive and other sexual and reproductive health services. 38. HIV testing serves as a first step in linking individuals to ART for those testing HIV-positive and to condom promotion and, where appropriate, PrEP for those testing HIV-negative. 39. The numerator is the number of adolescent girls and women seeking contraception or family planning services who were tested for HIV. 40. The denominator is the number of adolescent girls and women seeking contraception or family planning services. 41. Measurement methods for the numerator and denominator include program records and registers of contraception/sexual/reproductive health clinics. 42. Currently, HIV testing and referral to prevention or treatment are infrequently captured by reproductive health services. 43. New strategies and materials for collecting this indicator may be needed. 44. The intended focus of this indicator is adolescent girls and young women aged 10–24 years, assessed by reviewing results by 5-year age bands up to the age of 24 years. 45. The broader inclusion of women of reproductive age over the age of 25 serves as a comparison to identify trends among adolescent girls and young women. 46. Disaggregation includes age (10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–49, 50+) and HIV test status (negative, positive, indeterminate). 47. Additional recommendations for settings with robust electronic health information systems (e.g., EMRs) include referral to or uptake of prevention (e.g., PrEP) and treatment services that may reduce new infections, as well as HIV testing approaches (e.g., rapid diagnostic test, HIV self-testing, referral to HTS). 48. The number of voluntary medical male circumcisions (VMMCs) performed according to the national standard measures progress in scaling up male circumcision services. 49. WHO and UNAIDS recommend male circumcision as an effective intervention for HIV prevention in countries with heterosexual epidemics, high HIV prevalence, and low male circumcision prevalence. 50. Randomized controlled trials have shown that male circumcision provided by trained health professionals with proper equipment can reduce the risk of men heterosexually acquiring HIV infection. 51. The numerator is the number of voluntary medical male circumcisions performed during the reporting period according to the national standard. 52. Measurement methods include program data, such as VMMC registers. 53. The recommended reporting period is 12 months. 54. Disaggregation includes age (0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–49, 50+) and HIV status (positive, negative, indeterminate). 55. The number and percentage of circumcised males experiencing adverse events measure whether the scale-up of male circumcision services meets national standards of safety and effectiveness. 56. Staff conducting medical circumcisions must have appropriate training and access to proper equipment. 57. Trends in adverse events may indicate where service providers need additional support. 58. The numerator is the number of males experiencing at least one moderate or severe adverse event (e.g., complications resulting in death, hospitalization within 30 days, or permanent disability) during or following circumcision surgery in the reporting period. 59. The denominator is the number of men undergoing voluntary medical male circumcision during the reporting period. 60. Measurement methods for the numerator include program records, such as VMMC registers. 61. Intraoperative adverse events may include pain, excessive bleeding, anesthesia-related effects, excessive skin removal, damage to the penis, or sharps injury to personnel. 62. Postoperative adverse events may include abnormal pain, excessive swelling, infection, hematoma, bleeding, difficulty urinating, wound disruption, scarring or disfigurement, injury to the glans, or excessive skin removal. 63. Disaggregation includes age (0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–49, 50+), timing of adverse event (intraoperative, postoperative), and service site. 64. The percentage of healthcare facilities where all therapeutic injections are given with new, disposable, single-use injection equipment measures the implementation of policies to ensure injection safety. 65. Unsafe injections remain a concern in some countries, particularly those with high rates of unsafe injections per person per year or a prevalence of HCV infection greater than 2%. 66. The numerator is the number of sampled healthcare facilities where all therapeutic injections are given with new, disposable, single-use injection equipment. 67. The denominator is the number of facilities sampled. 68. Measurement methods for the numerator and denominator include health facility surveys. 69. Disaggregation includes the type of site. 70. The rate of unsafe healthcare injections per person measures the extent of unsafe healthcare injections in a population and allows for monitoring of trends. 71. While the risk of HIV transmission from unsafe healthcare injections has decreased globally, it remains a priority in some countries. 72. The numerator is the average number of unsafe healthcare injections during one year among survey respondents. 73. The denominator is the number of survey respondents who answer the question. 74. Measurement methods for the numerator and denominator include general population surveys (e.g., DHS, PHIA, AIS). 75. The numerator is calculated by multiplying the response from Q1 by the proportion who answer “no” to Q2. 76. Q1: “Have you had an injection for any reason in the last 12 months?” 77. Disaggregation includes gender (male, female, transgender) and age (<15, 15+). 78. The percentage of health facilities providing blood transfusion that meet requirements for safe and sufficient blood transfusion measures the effectiveness of policies and programs to ensure a safe and adequate blood supply. 79. While the risk of HIV transmission from unsafe blood transfusion has decreased globally, it remains a priority in some countries. 80. The numerator is the number of health facilities providing blood transfusion with tracer items on the day of the assessment by the Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA) survey indicators index. 81. The denominator is the number of surveyed health facilities providing blood transfusion. 82. Measurement methods for the numerator and denominator include health facility surveys (SARA). 83. Disaggregation includes the type of site. 84. The percentage of blood units that are screened for bloodborne diseases in a quality-assured manner measures the extent of quality-assured screening of blood units at different levels of the health system. 85. Unsafe blood transfusion is still a concern, especially in lowand middle-income countries where the prevalence of transfusion-transmissible infections is high and the quality and coverage of blood screening are inadequate. 86. Less than 100% screening indicates a lack of or inappropriate laboratory screening and flags the risk of transmission through unsafe blood supplies. 87. The numerator is the number of donated blood units tested in a quality-assured manner for HIV, HBV, HCV, and syphilis. 88. The denominator is the number of donated blood units. 89. Measurement methods for the numerator and denominator include health facility surveys. 90. Disaggregation includes facility type and location (e.g., region, district). 91. Further information can be found in the Global Health Sector Strategy on HIV (2016–2021) and the Global Hepatitis Report (2017). 92. The percentage of people living with HIV newly initiated on ART who were screened for TB measures the extent to which individuals newly initiated on ART are screened for active TB disease. 93. Routine TB screening among people living with HIV newly initiated on ART and those already on ART is essential to identify presumptive TB cases in need of confirmatory diagnostic testing and to determine eligibility for TPT if active TB disease is ruled out. 94. Screening is most critical at the time of ART initiation, when immune compromise is greatest.
